goals: Explain the features of perfect competition and why the firm is a price taker
Explain interdependence in oligopoly and the meaning of monopsony

slides.heading: Market Forms
slides.body_md: Part 1 — how markets differ in **number of sellers**, **product**, **entry** and **control over price**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: perfect competition, monopoly, monopolistic competition, oligopoly and the meaning of monopsony
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: A wheat grower at a mandi, the only ferry to an island, a street of sweet shops and four big cement makers all sell goods, but their markets work very differently. In this part we learn to tell market forms apart by the number of sellers, the kind of product, the freedom to enter, and how much each firm controls its price.

slides.heading: Four market forms at a glance

visual.alt: Comparison table of four market forms by number of sellers, product, entry, control over price and selling costs: perfect competition has very many sellers of an identical product with free entry and no price control; monopoly has one seller with barriers and full control; monopolistic competition has many sellers of differentiated products with free entry and some control; oligopoly has a few interdependent sellers with difficult entry

slides.narration: Here are the four main market forms side by side. Read across each row. Perfect competition has very many sellers of an identical product. A monopoly has a single seller. Monopolistic competition has many sellers of slightly different products. An oligopoly has only a few sellers who watch each other closely. Keep this table in mind for every question in the chapter.

slides.heading: Perfect competition: the features

headers: Why it makes the firm a price taker
rows: Each firm's output is a tiny part of supply
A higher price loses all buyers to rivals
No firm keeps a special position for long
Everyone knows the one ruling price
Factors move to where they earn most

visual.alt: Table of the features of perfect competition and how each makes the firm a price taker: very many sellers, homogeneous product, free entry and exit, perfect knowledge and perfect mobility of factors

slides.narration: Perfect competition rests on a set of features. There are so many buyers and sellers that each is tiny. The product of every seller is the same. Firms can enter and leave freely. Everyone knows the ruling price, and factors move freely. The right-hand column shows how each feature takes away the firm's power over price.

slides.heading: Quick check: knowledge and price
slides.body_md: Does perfect knowledge help keep one uniform price?
slides.narration: Imagine a buyer who did not know the price elsewhere. Could a seller charge him more? Now imagine everyone knows.

visual.caption: The industry sets the price; the firm takes it.

slides.narration: On the left, the market demand and supply for the whole industry decide the price, here forty. On the right, one firm faces that price as a flat line. It can sell as much as it wants at forty but nothing above it, so its average revenue and marginal revenue are both equal to the price. We call it a price taker.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: reading a market
slides.body_md: At an imagined Hisar wheat mandi, thousands of growers sell grain of one grade at a price called out by the market. Identify the market form and give two reasons.
bullets: Step 1 — Count the sellers: thousands.
Step 2 — Look at the product: one grade, identical.
Step 3 — Who sets the price? The market, not any grower.
Step 4 — Conclude: perfect competition; quote the evidence.

rows: Hundreds of sellers, same grade, price on a board
Only one seller; licence keeps others out
Many sellers, own brands, new shops opening
A few big firms reacting to each other

visual.alt: Table of clues for identifying a market form in a case: many sellers of the same grade point to perfect competition; one protected seller to monopoly; many branded sellers with new entrants to monopolistic competition; a few reacting firms to oligopoly; one buyer to monopsony
visual.caption: Quote the line that gives the clue.

slides.narration: Go through the clues one by one. Thousands of sellers means each is tiny. Grain of one grade means the product is identical. The price is called out by the market, so no grower sets it. All three point to perfect competition. In the exam, name the form and quote the words that prove each feature.

slides.heading: Monopoly and monopolistic competition
columns: **Monopoly:** one seller, **no close substitute**, **barriers** to entry, price maker.
**Monopolistic competition:** many sellers, **differentiated** products, **free entry**, **selling costs**.

rows: Some control over its own price
Imagined example: an island's only licensed ferry
Imagined example: two hundred branded knitwear shops

visual.alt: Table comparing monopoly with monopolistic competition: one seller versus many; no close substitute versus differentiated substitutes; barriers versus free entry; price maker versus some price control; with an imagined ferry monopoly and an imagined knitwear market as examples

slides.narration: A monopoly is a single seller whose product has no close substitute, protected by barriers such as a licence or patent, so it can make the price. Monopolistic competition has many sellers whose products are similar but made different by brand, design or packing. Entry is free, and firms spend on advertising to win buyers.

slides.heading: Quick check: what protects a monopoly?
slides.body_md: Which of these helps a monopolist keep supernormal profit even in the long run?
slides.narration: Ask what stops rivals from entering and competing the profit away.

visual.alt: Three small panels of the demand (average revenue) curve facing one firm: horizontal under perfect competition; steep and downward sloping for a monopolist, which faces the whole market demand; downward sloping but flatter (more elastic) under monopolistic competition, because close substitutes exist
visual.caption: Perfectly elastic; less elastic; more elastic.

slides.narration: Compare the demand curve each firm faces. Under perfect competition it is flat at the market price. A monopolist faces the whole market demand, which slopes down steeply. A firm under monopolistic competition faces a downward slope too, but a flatter one, because buyers can switch to close substitutes if it raises its price.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: differentiating a product
slides.body_md: An imagined Kolkata sweet shop wants buyers to choose its rasgullas over those of nearby shops. Suggest how, and name the market form.
bullets: Step 1 — Many shops sell close substitutes: monopolistic competition.
Step 2 — Differentiate: recipe, packing, brand name.
Step 3 — Spend on selling costs: signboards, offers.
Step 4 — Result: some loyal buyers and a little control over price.

rows: Some control over its own price
Imagined example: an island's only licensed ferry
Imagined example: two hundred branded knitwear shops

visual.alt: Table comparing monopoly with monopolistic competition: one seller versus many; no close substitute versus differentiated substitutes; barriers versus free entry; price maker versus some price control; with an imagined ferry monopoly and an imagined knitwear market as examples

slides.narration: Many shops on one street sell similar sweets, so this is monopolistic competition. The shop can make its rasgullas different through a special recipe, attractive boxes and a memorable name, and it can spend on signboards and offers. If buyers come to prefer it, the shop gains some control over its own price.

slides.heading: Oligopoly: a few interdependent sellers
slides.body_md: A few large sellers; each **watches and reacts** to the others. Its demand curve is **indeterminate**.

nodes.label: One cement maker cuts its price
First firm's sales depend on that choice

visual.alt: Flow showing interdependence in an imagined four-firm cement oligopoly: one firm cuts its price, rivals lose buyers, they decide whether to follow, and the first firm's sales depend on their choice
visual.caption: Interdependence: the key feature of oligopoly

slides.narration: In an oligopoly only a few big firms supply the market. If one cement maker cuts its price, its rivals lose buyers and must decide how to respond. Because the first firm cannot know what they will do, it cannot be sure how much it will sell. That is why we say its demand curve is indeterminate.

slides.heading: Quick check: the mark of oligopoly
slides.body_md: What is the most distinctive feature of oligopoly?
slides.narration: Think about what makes a few big firms different from a monopoly and from many small firms.

slides.heading: Monopsony: meaning only

rows: The only ferry to an island
The only sugar mill buying a valley's cane

visual.alt: Table contrasting monopoly, a market with one seller such as an island's only ferry, with monopsony, a market with one buyer such as the only sugar mill buying cane in a valley
visual.caption: Monopsony: meaning only in the ISC syllabus.

slides.narration: Do not confuse monopoly with monopsony. A monopoly has one seller. A monopsony has one buyer, such as the only sugar mill buying cane from all the growers of a valley. For the syllabus you need only its meaning and an example.

slides.heading: Quick check: one buyer
slides.body_md: Complete the term for a market with only one buyer.
slides.narration: The word sounds like monopoly but is about buying, not selling.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: Many sellers, identical product, free entry; firm is a price taker
One seller, no close substitute, barriers; price maker
Many sellers, differentiated products, selling costs
A few interdependent sellers; demand curve indeterminate

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: the features of perfect competition, monopoly, monopolistic competition and oligopoly, and the meaning of monopsony

slides.narration: To sum up Part 1. Under perfect competition many sellers of an identical product make each firm a price taker. A monopolist is the only seller and a price maker. Monopolistic competition has many sellers of differentiated brands. Oligopoly has a few sellers who depend on each other. Monopsony means a single buyer.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Identify the market form from **evidence** and **quote** the line that shows it.
Monopoly = one **seller**; monopsony = one **buyer**.
Under perfect competition **AR = MR = price**: a horizontal line.
Oligopoly's key word is **interdependence**; monopolistic competition's is **product differentiation**.
Compare forms on fixed bases: sellers, product, entry, price control, selling costs.

visual.alt: Comparison table of four market forms by number of sellers, product, entry, control over price and selling costs: perfect competition has very many sellers of an identical product with free entry and no price control; monopoly has one seller with barriers and full control; monopolistic competition has many sellers of differentiated products with free entry and some control; oligopoly has a few interdependent sellers with difficult entry

slides.narration: In case questions, name the form and quote the words that prove it. Keep monopoly and monopsony apart. Remember that a competitive firm's revenue curves are one flat line. Use the key word for each form: interdependence for oligopoly and product differentiation for monopolistic competition. When comparing, use the same bases for each form.

decks.title: Market Forms — Part 2: Equilibrium of a Firm under Perfect Competition
goals: State the conditions of a competitive firm's short-run equilibrium
Show supernormal profit, normal profit and loss with diagrams
Identify the break-even and shut-down points and explain long-run normal profit

slides.heading: Equilibrium of a Competitive Firm
slides.body_md: Part 2 — how a price taker chooses its output, when it earns **profit**, **normal profit** or a **loss**, and when it **shuts down**.

nodes.label: Market price given: AR = MR = P

visual.alt: Flow of a competitive firm's short-run decision: take the market price as average and marginal revenue, find the output where marginal cost equals marginal revenue, check marginal cost is rising, check price covers average variable cost, then produce or shut down

slides.narration: A firm under perfect competition cannot choose its price, but it can choose how much to produce. In this part we find the output that gives the most profit, see when that profit is large, normal or negative, and learn the price below which the firm should stop producing in the short run.

slides.heading: Two conditions of equilibrium
bullets: **MC = MR:** the last unit adds as much to cost as to revenue.
**MC rising:** MC cuts MR from below, so units beyond it would lose money.
For a price taker, MR = AR = price.

nodes.label: Market price given: AR = MR = P

visual.alt: Flow of a competitive firm's short-run decision: take the market price as average and marginal revenue, find the output where marginal cost equals marginal revenue, check marginal cost is rising, check price covers average variable cost, then produce or shut down

slides.narration: A firm earns the most profit when the last unit adds just as much to cost as to revenue: marginal cost equals marginal revenue. That point must also be on the rising part of marginal cost, so that any further unit would cost more than it brings in. For a competitive firm, marginal revenue is simply the market price.

slides.body_md: An imagined Erode turmeric-powder unit (fixed cost ₹36) faces prices of ₹33, ₹24 and ₹18. Decide its output at each.
bullets: Step 1 — MC from the schedule: 24, 18, 15, 18, 24, 33.
Step 2 — At each price, find MC = MR with MC rising.
Step 3 — Profit = TR − TC.
Step 4 — Compare any loss with the fixed cost of ₹36.

visual.caption: Shut down only if price < minimum AVC (₹18.75).

At twenty-four the best output is five, with a loss of fifteen, less than the fixed cost of thirty-six, so it keeps producing. At eighteen the best output would lose thirty-nine, more than closing, so it shuts down.

slides.body_md: The brass unit has minimum AVC ₹15 hundred and minimum AC ₹28 hundred. Classify prices of ₹47, ₹28, ₹20 and ₹12 hundred.
bullets: Above 28: supernormal profit.
Equal to 28: normal profit.
Between 15 and 28: loss but produce.
Below 15: shut down.

slides.narration: Place each price against the two key numbers, the lowest average variable cost of fifteen and the lowest average cost of twenty-eight. Forty-seven is above both, so there is supernormal profit. Twenty-eight gives normal profit. Twenty lies between them, so there is a loss but the firm produces. Twelve is below fifteen, so the firm shuts down.

slides.heading: Quick check: the long run
slides.body_md: In the long run, a firm under perfect competition earns…
slides.narration: Think about what free entry and exit do to any extra profit or loss.

slides.heading: Long-run equilibrium (explanation only)
bullets: Supernormal profit → **entry** → supply rises → price falls.
Losses → **exit** → supply falls → price rises.
Adjustment stops at **P = minimum average cost**: normal profit only.

visual.alt: Flow of long-run adjustment under perfect competition: supernormal profit attracts new firms, market supply rises, price falls, and entry stops when price equals minimum average cost with only normal profit; losses work the other way through exit
visual.caption: Losses reverse the chain through exit (explanation only; no diagram).

slides.narration: In the long run firms can enter and leave. If they earn supernormal profit, newcomers arrive, supply rises and the price falls. If they make losses, some leave, supply falls and the price rises. The movement stops only when price equals the lowest average cost, so every firm earns just normal profit. The syllabus asks for this explanation, not a diagram.

slides.heading: Quick check: price in the long run
slides.body_md: In long-run equilibrium, does price equal minimum long-run average cost?
slides.narration: If price were above it, what would new firms do? If below, what would existing firms do?

rows: MC = MR = P with MC rising
Entry and exit leave only normal profit

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 2: the equilibrium conditions, supernormal profit, the break-even point, the shut-down point and long-run normal profit

slides.narration: To sum up Part 2. A competitive firm produces where marginal cost equals the price and is rising. If price is above average cost it earns supernormal profit; at the lowest average cost it breaks even; between the lowest average variable cost and the lowest average cost it makes a loss but produces; below the lowest average variable cost it shuts down. In the long run only normal profit remains.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: State **both** conditions: MC = MR **and** MC rising.
Profit = (AR − AC) × Q, or TR − TC; show the rectangle in the diagram.
Break-even = minimum **AC**; shut-down = minimum **AVC**. Do not swap them.
A loss alone is no reason to close: compare the loss with **fixed cost**.
Long-run equilibrium: **explain** entry and exit; no diagram is needed.

slides.narration: Always give both equilibrium conditions. Work profit as the gap between average revenue and average cost times output, or as total revenue minus total cost. Keep break-even at the lowest average cost and shut-down at the lowest average variable cost. Before advising a firm to close, compare its loss with its fixed cost. For the long run, explain in words.

sections.heading: 1. Perfect competition
sections.body_md:
**Features:** very many buyers and sellers; homogeneous product; free entry and exit; perfect knowledge; perfect mobility of factors; no selling costs.

**Consequence:** the industry fixes the price by market demand and supply; each firm is a **price taker** and can sell any quantity at that price. Its demand curve is **perfectly elastic**: **AR = MR = price**, one horizontal line.

key_terms.definition_md: A firm that must accept the price set by the market because its own output cannot affect it.
A product that buyers regard as identical whichever firm sells it.

rows: Each firm's output is a tiny part of supply
A higher price loses all buyers to rivals
No firm keeps a special position for long
Everyone knows the one ruling price
Factors move to where they earn most

sections.heading: 2. Monopoly and monopolistic competition
sections.body_md:
**Monopoly:** a single seller; no close substitute; strong **barriers to entry** (licence, patent, control of an input, huge capital); **price maker**; may practise price discrimination; demand curve is the downward-sloping market demand.

**Monopolistic competition:** many sellers; **product differentiation** (brand, design, packing); free entry and exit; **selling costs**; some control over its own price; demand slopes down but is more elastic than a monopolist's.

key_terms.definition_md: Making a product appear different from rivals' close substitutes through brand, design, quality or packing.
Spending to promote sales, such as advertising and displays.

sections.heading: 3. Oligopoly; monopsony
sections.body_md:
**Oligopoly:** a few large sellers; **interdependence** in pricing and output decisions; barriers to entry; heavy advertising; the firm's demand curve is **indeterminate**, because its sales depend on rivals' unknown reactions.

**Monopsony** (meaning only): a market with a **single buyer**, such as the only mill buying a district's cane.

key_terms.definition_md: The dependence of each oligopolist's decisions on the expected reactions of its rivals.
A market with only one buyer of a good or factor.

First firm's sales depend on that choice

sections.heading: 4. Short-run equilibrium of a competitive firm
sections.body_md:
**Conditions:** MC = MR (= AR = P) and MC rising (cutting MR from below).

- **Supernormal profit:** P above AC at the equilibrium output; profit = (AR − AC) × Q.
- **Normal profit:** P = minimum AC; TR = TC.
- **Loss:** P below AC but above AVC; the firm still produces.

key_terms.definition_md: Profit above normal profit; total revenue exceeds total cost.
The minimum return that keeps an entrepreneur in the industry; included in average cost.

sections.heading: 5. Break-even and shut-down points
sections.body_md:
**Break-even point:** P = minimum AC (brass unit: ₹28 hundred at 6 hundred fittings).

**Shut-down point:** P = minimum AVC (brass unit: ₹15 hundred at 5 hundred fittings). Below it, revenue fails to cover variable cost and the firm stops producing; at it, the loss equals fixed cost.

**From a schedule:** find MC = MR with MC rising; compute TR − TC; if the loss exceeds TFC, shut down (imagined turmeric unit: shut down below ₹18.75).

key_terms.definition_md: The output and price at which a firm's total revenue equals total cost, so it earns only normal profit.
The price equal to minimum average variable cost, below which a firm stops production in the short run.

sections.heading: 6. Long-run equilibrium (explanation only)
sections.body_md: Supernormal profit attracts **new firms** (free entry); market supply rises and price falls. Losses make some firms **leave** (free exit); supply falls and price rises. In the long run **P = AR = MR = MC = minimum LAC**, and every firm earns **only normal profit**. (The long-run diagram is not required by the ISC 2027 syllabus.)

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Calling monopsony a market with one seller.
- Giving only MC = MR and forgetting that MC must be rising.
- Treating every loss as a reason to close: compare the loss with fixed cost.
- Swapping the break-even point (minimum AC) and the shut-down point (minimum AVC).
- Drawing the competitive firm's demand curve sloping down.
- Drawing a long-run diagram when the question asks for an explanation.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1 mark: one correct option, term or value.
- 2 marks: two features, or a condition with its reason.
- 3 marks: three bases of comparison, or a described diagram with the key point.
- 5 marks: parts answered in order, with described diagrams, working from schedules and a clear decision.

Entry → supply up → price down → **normal profit**.
Exit → supply down → price up → **normal profit**.
P = minimum **LAC**; explanation only, no diagram needed.

questions.stem_md: At an imagined wheat mandi near Hisar, thousands of growers sell grain of the same grade and none can change the ruling price by selling more or less. This market is closest to

options.text_md: monopoly
perfect competition
oligopoly
monopolistic competition

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** perfect competition. Very many sellers, an identical product and no single seller able to affect price are the marks of perfect competition. Monopoly has one seller, oligopoly a few interdependent sellers, and monopolistic competition differentiated products.

questions.stem_md: A firm under perfect competition is called a price taker because

options.text_md: the government fixes the price of its product
it must charge the lowest price among its rivals
it sells only to a single large buyer
its output is too small a part of the market to affect the price set by industry demand and supply

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** its output is too small a part of the market to affect the price set by industry demand and supply. Price is set by market (industry) demand and supply; each firm's output is tiny compared with the market, so it accepts that price. The government and a single buyer play no part in the definition.

questions.stem_md: For a firm selling at a market-given price of ₹47 under perfect competition, which statement about its revenue curves is correct?

options.text_md: AR = MR = ₹47, a horizontal line
AR is ₹47 but MR is below it and falling
MR is ₹47 but AR rises with output
AR and MR both slope downward from ₹47

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** AR = MR = ₹47, a horizontal line. Every extra unit sells at the same ₹47, so marginal revenue equals the price and so does average revenue; both are one horizontal line at the market price.

questions.stem_md: Buyers at an imagined cotton market in Akola treat every seller's bales of the same grade as identical. Which consequence of this feature is most direct?

options.text_md: Every seller must spend heavily on advertising
New sellers cannot enter the market
No seller can charge more than others without losing all buyers
Sellers watch and react to each other's prices

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** No seller can charge more than others without losing all buyers. With a homogeneous product a buyer has no reason to pay any seller more, so a higher price loses all custom: the firm must accept the market price. Heavy advertising, entry barriers and mutual reactions belong to other market forms.

questions.stem_md: Free entry and exit under perfect competition matter mainly because they

options.text_md: allow each firm to set its own price
make the product differentiated
remove supernormal profit and losses in the long run
let the firm earn supernormal profit for ever

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** remove supernormal profit and losses in the long run. If firms earn supernormal profit, new firms enter and price falls; if they make losses, some leave and price rises. Either way, in the long run only normal profit remains.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The demand curve facing a single firm under perfect competition is perfectly elastic.

**Reason (R):** The firm can sell any quantity it wishes at the ruling market price, but nothing at all at a higher price.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: since buyers will pay only the market price and will take any amount the small firm offers at it, the firm's demand curve is horizontal, that is, perfectly elastic.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Perfect knowledge of market prices by buyers and sellers helps keep one uniform price throughout a perfectly competitive market.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** If everyone knows the ruling price, no buyer pays more and no seller accepts less, so a single price prevails.

questions.stem_md: Under perfect competition the price is fixed by the industry, and each firm is a price ___.
questions.solution_md: The industry sets the price; the firm is a price taker.

questions.stem_md: An imagined Jalgaon banana grower in a perfectly competitive market sells 1,200 dozen at the market price of ₹30 a dozen. What is his total revenue in ₹?
Explain any two features of perfect competition, using an imagined onion market at Lasalgaon as your example.
questions.solution_md: Two features linked to the onion market.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Very many sellers and buyers:** thousands of Lasalgaon growers each sell a **tiny share**, so none can move the price.
2. **Homogeneous product:** onions of a grade are **identical**, so buyers will not pay one grower more than another.

questions.stem_md: Why would a grower at an imagined Hisar wheat mandi gain nothing by advertising his grain? Answer with reference to perfect competition.
questions.solution_md: Homogeneous product, perfect knowledge and unlimited sales at the market price.

answer.model_answer_md: His grain is **identical** to everyone else's, buyers already have **perfect knowledge** of the price, and he can sell **all he wants** at the ruling price. Advertising would only **add to cost** without raising his price or sales.

marking_scheme.step: Can sell any amount anyway; cost only

questions.stem_md: Explain three features of perfect competition and show how each one makes the firm a price taker.
questions.solution_md: Three features, each linked to price taking.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Large number of sellers:** each firm's output is a **negligible** part of market supply, so changing it cannot shift the price.
2. **Homogeneous product:** buyers see no difference between firms, so a firm charging more **loses all buyers**.
3. **Perfect knowledge:** buyers know the ruling price everywhere, so **no seller** can charge above it unnoticed. Together these leave the firm only to **accept** the market price.

marking_scheme.step: Many sellers linked to price taking

questions.stem_md: An imagined island district has one ferry company, licensed by law as the only carrier to the mainland, with no other way to cross. Its market form is

options.text_md: monopoly
perfect competition
monopolistic competition
monopsony

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** monopoly. A single seller, no close substitute and a legal barrier to entry make it a monopoly. Monopsony means a single buyer, not a single seller.

questions.stem_md: An imagined Ludhiana market has over two hundred knitwear shops; each sells sweaters with its own designs and label, and anyone can open a new shop. This is an example of

options.text_md: oligopoly
perfect competition
monopoly
monopolistic competition

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** monopolistic competition. Many sellers, free entry and differentiated products are the marks of monopolistic competition. Perfect competition needs identical products; oligopoly has only a few sellers.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following helps a monopolist keep supernormal profit even in the long run?

options.text_md: A perfectly elastic demand curve
Barriers that stop new firms from entering
A large number of rival sellers
Perfect knowledge among buyers

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Barriers that stop new firms from entering. Barriers to entry (licences, patents, control of a key input, huge set-up cost) keep rivals out, so profit is not competed away. The other options describe competitive conditions.

questions.stem_md: Spending by an imagined Kanpur shoe-maker on hoardings and free gifts to show its brand is better than rivals' brands is an example of selling costs. Such costs are most typical of

options.text_md: monopolistic competition
perfect competition
a pure monopoly with no substitutes
a monopsony

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** monopolistic competition. With differentiated products, firms spend on advertising to persuade buyers their brand is different and better. Under perfect competition products are identical, so there is no point in selling costs.

questions.stem_md: Compared with a monopolist's demand curve, the demand curve of a firm under monopolistic competition is

options.text_md: less elastic, because brand loyalty is total
more elastic, because each brand has many close substitutes
horizontal, because the product is homogeneous
vertical, because the firm fixes output

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** more elastic, because each brand has many close substitutes. Both slope downward, but a monopolistically competitive firm faces many close substitutes, so a price rise loses more buyers: its demand is more elastic. A monopolist has no close substitutes.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A monopolist is a price maker.

**Reason (R):** As the sole seller of a product with no close substitutes, the monopolist faces the whole market demand curve and can choose a price on it.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: facing the downward-sloping market demand, the monopolist can fix the price (and sell what is demanded at it) instead of accepting a given price.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Firms under monopolistic competition have some control over the price of their own product.

**Reason (R):** Entry of new firms into monopolistic competition is blocked by law.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A is true: product differentiation gives each firm a small, loyal group of buyers and some price-setting power. R is false: entry and exit are free under monopolistic competition.

questions.stem_md: True or false? A monopolist may be able to charge different prices to different groups of buyers for the same product.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** With no rivals to undercut it, a monopolist can practise price discrimination when buyers can be separated and cannot resell, for example charging different rates to different classes of users.

questions.stem_md: Match each feature with the market form in which it is the defining mark.

options.text_md: Identical product sold by very many firms
Single seller, no close substitutes
Many sellers of differentiated brands
A few sellers who react to each other

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(p), (c)–(s), (d)–(q). Homogeneous product with many firms marks perfect competition; one seller marks monopoly; differentiated products with many sellers mark monopolistic competition; interdependence among a few sellers marks oligopoly.

questions.stem_md: State two features of monopoly and give an imagined Indian example for each.
questions.solution_md: Two features, each with an example.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Single seller with no close substitutes:** an imagined state power utility is the only supplier of electricity in its area.
2. **Barriers to entry:** a licence or patent keeps rivals out, as when an imagined firm holds the only patent for a new seed.

questions.stem_md: What is product differentiation? Show how an imagined Kolkata sweet shop might differentiate its rasgullas from those of the shops on the same street.
questions.solution_md: Meaning plus specific ways of differentiating.

answer.model_answer_md: **Product differentiation** means making a product **appear different** from rivals' close substitutes. The Kolkata shop could use a **distinct recipe and flavour**, **attractive branded boxes** and a **name** buyers remember, so some buyers prefer its rasgullas even at a slightly higher price.

marking_scheme.step: Specific ways for the sweet shop

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between monopoly and monopolistic competition on the basis of number of sellers, nature of the product and entry of new firms.
questions.solution_md: Three bases, both forms on each.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Sellers:** monopoly has a **single** seller; monopolistic competition has **many** sellers.
2. **Product:** a monopolist's product has **no close substitute**; under monopolistic competition products are **close substitutes** made different by brand, design or packing.
3. **Entry:** monopoly is protected by **strong barriers**; under monopolistic competition **entry and exit are free**, so supernormal profit tends to disappear in the long run.

questions.stem_md: Using the imagined knitwear market of Ludhiana with over two hundred branded shops, explain three features of monopolistic competition.
questions.solution_md: Three features applied to the knitwear market.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Many sellers:** over two hundred shops compete, so no one dominates the market.
2. **Product differentiation:** each shop's sweaters carry **its own designs and label**, so buyers see them as close but **not perfect** substitutes.
3. **Selling costs and free entry:** shops spend on **displays and advertising**, and a newcomer can **open freely**, which keeps long-run profit near normal.

questions.stem_md: Explain three ways in which an imagined monopoly, such as the only maker of a patented water-purifier membrane, can keep rival firms out of its market.
questions.solution_md: Three barriers to entry, each explained.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Patent:** the law gives the firm the **sole right** to make the patented membrane for some years, so rivals cannot copy it.
2. **Control of a key input:** if it owns the only source of a vital material, others **cannot obtain** it.
3. **Huge set-up cost:** a new plant needs **very large capital**, so a newcomer cannot easily match the monopolist's **low cost** at a large scale.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between perfect competition and monopoly on five bases, with an imagined Indian example of each market.
questions.solution_md: Five bases, both forms on each.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Sellers:** perfect competition has **very many** sellers, as at an imagined grain mandi; a monopoly has **one**, as an imagined island's only ferry service.
2. **Product:** competitive sellers offer an **identical** product; the monopolist's product has **no close substitute**.
3. **Entry:** entry and exit are **free** under perfect competition; a monopoly is protected by **barriers** such as a licence.
4. **Price:** the competitive firm is a **price taker**; the monopolist is a **price maker** who may even charge different buyers different prices.
5. **Demand and profit:** the competitive firm's demand is **horizontal** (AR = MR) and only normal profit survives in the long run; the monopolist's demand **slopes down** (MR below AR) and supernormal profit can **last**.

questions.stem_md: Four large cement makers supply an imagined state; when one announces a price cut, the other three quickly decide how to respond. The market form shown is

options.text_md: monopoly
perfect competition
oligopoly
monopolistic competition

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** oligopoly. A few large sellers whose decisions depend on one another's reactions mark oligopoly. Interdependence is its key feature.

questions.stem_md: The most distinctive feature of oligopoly is

options.text_md: a homogeneous product sold by very many firms
a single seller with no rivals
free entry with no selling costs
interdependence of the firms in decision-making

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** interdependence of the firms in decision-making. With only a few sellers, each firm's price or output decision affects its rivals and invites a reaction, so firms are interdependent.

questions.stem_md: In an imagined hill valley the only buyer of sugarcane from hundreds of growers is a single sugar mill. The mill's position in the cane market is called

options.text_md: monopoly
oligopoly
duopoly
monopsony

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** monopsony. Monopsony is a market with a single buyer. The mill buys all the cane, so it is a monopsonist; monopoly means a single seller.

questions.stem_md: Why is it hard to draw a definite demand curve for one firm in an oligopoly?

options.text_md: Its product has no substitutes at all
The government fixes its sales
The quantity it sells at a price depends on how its rivals react, which is uncertain
Its buyers have perfect knowledge of all prices

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The quantity it sells at a price depends on how its rivals react, which is uncertain. A firm's sales after a price change depend on whether rivals follow or not; since their reaction cannot be known in advance, the firm's demand curve is indeterminate.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Oligopoly firms often spend large sums on advertising.

**Reason (R):** Oligopoly has only a few sellers.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both are true, but R does not explain A. Heavy advertising arises because firms compete for market share without starting price wars, and each tries to make its product appear different; merely having few sellers does not by itself explain it.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Monopsony is a market with a single seller.

**Reason (R):** Under monopsony the sole buyer has no influence on the price it pays.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Both are false. Monopsony is a market with a single buyer, and that buyer has considerable influence on the price it pays because sellers have nowhere else to sell.

questions.stem_md: A market in which there is only one buyer of a product or factor is called ___.
questions.solution_md: A single buyer: monopsony.

questions.stem_md: Explain two features of oligopoly using an imagined market for two-wheelers dominated by four makers.
questions.solution_md: Two features linked to the two-wheeler market.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Few large sellers:** four makers supply most two-wheelers, so each has a **big market share**.
2. **Interdependence:** if one maker **cuts its price** or launches a new model, the others must **react**, so each plans while watching its rivals.

questions.stem_md: What is meant by monopsony? Give an imagined example from a rural labour market.
questions.solution_md: Meaning and a single-buyer example.

answer.model_answer_md: **Monopsony** is a market with **only one buyer** of a good or factor. Example: in an imagined plantation village the **only employer** hires all the farm workers, so the workers have **no other buyer** for their labour.

questions.stem_md: Compare oligopoly with perfect competition on three bases of your choice.
questions.solution_md: Three bases, contrasting both forms.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Number of sellers:** perfect competition has **very many** sellers; oligopoly has **only a few** large ones.
2. **Pricing:** a competitive firm is a **price taker**; an oligopolist has influence over price but must consider **rivals' reactions**.
3. **Selling costs and entry:** competitive firms spend **nothing** on advertising and entry is **free**; oligopolists spend **heavily** on advertising and **barriers** make entry hard.

questions.stem_md: A perfectly competitive firm is in short-run equilibrium when

options.text_md: AC is at its minimum, whatever the price
MC = MR and MC is rising at that output
TR is at its maximum
MR is greater than MC by the largest amount

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** MC = MR and MC is rising at that output. Profit is greatest where an extra unit adds as much to cost as to revenue (MC = MR) and beyond which MC exceeds MR, which requires MC to cut MR from below (MC rising).

questions.stem_md: For a perfectly competitive firm, the break-even point is reached when price equals

options.text_md: minimum average cost
minimum average variable cost
minimum marginal cost
average fixed cost

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** minimum average cost. At P = minimum AC, total revenue just covers total cost including normal profit, so the firm earns only normal profit: the break-even point.

questions.stem_md: An imagined Rajkot brass-fittings unit has AVC = Q² − 10Q + 40 and AC = AVC + 72/Q (₹ hundred, Q in hundreds). Its minimum AVC is ₹15 hundred and minimum AC is ₹28 hundred. Below which price will it stop production in the short run?

options.text_md: ₹28 hundred
₹15 hundred
₹13 hundred
₹72 hundred

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** ₹15 hundred. The shut-down point is where price equals minimum AVC, ₹15 hundred. Below it, revenue does not even cover variable cost, so producing loses more than the fixed cost of ₹72 hundred. Between ₹15 and ₹28 hundred it produces at a loss.

questions.stem_md: At a market price of ₹20 hundred, the imagined Rajkot unit's price is above its AVC but below its AC at the best output. In the short run it should

options.text_md: shut down at once, because it makes a loss
raise its price above the market price
produce where AC is lowest, ignoring MC
keep producing, because revenue covers variable cost and part of fixed cost

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** keep producing, because revenue covers variable cost and part of fixed cost. Fixed cost must be paid even at zero output. As price exceeds AVC, each unit adds something towards fixed cost, so producing makes a smaller loss than closing.

questions.stem_md: In the profit diagram of the imagined Rajkot unit, price is ₹47 hundred, output is 7 hundred and AC at that output is about ₹29.29 hundred. Its supernormal profit is about

options.text_md: ₹124 hundred
₹329 hundred
₹17.71 hundred
₹205 hundred

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** ₹124 hundred. Profit = (AR − AC) × Q = (47 − 29.29) × 7 ≈ 124, the same as TR − TC = 329 − 205. The per-unit gap alone is not total profit.

questions.stem_md: Normal profit, which a competitive firm earns at its break-even point, is best described as

options.text_md: any profit above average cost
a loss equal to fixed cost
the minimum return the owner needs to stay in the industry, included in average cost
the profit earned only by monopolists

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** the minimum return the owner needs to stay in the industry, included in average cost. Normal profit is the opportunity cost of the entrepreneur, the least return that keeps her in the business. Economists count it in cost, so at P = AC the firm earns exactly normal profit.

questions.stem_md: In the schedule of an imagined Erode turmeric-powder unit, MC equals the price of ₹24 both at the 1st and the 5th hundred packets. Why is the 1st not the equilibrium output?

options.text_md: Price is below AC at the 1st hundred packets
TR is zero at the 1st hundred packets
MC is falling there, so producing more units adds more to revenue than to cost
The firm cannot sell fewer than 500 packets

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** MC is falling there, so producing more units adds more to revenue than to cost. At the 1st hundred packets MC is about to fall, so the next units each add less to cost than the price: profit rises by producing more. The equilibrium needs MC = MR with MC rising, which happens at the 5th.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A competitive firm may continue to produce in the short run even when it makes a loss.

**Reason (R):** If price covers average variable cost, producing reduces the loss below the fixed cost that must be paid anyway.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: closing would leave a loss equal to total fixed cost; when P ≥ AVC, the revenue covers variable cost and some fixed cost, so the loss is smaller by producing.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** At the break-even point a competitive firm earns only normal profit.

**Reason (R):** Marginal cost cuts average cost at its lowest point.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both are true, but R does not explain A. A holds because at the break-even point price equals AC, so TR equals TC (which includes normal profit). R is a general property of cost curves; it explains why the break-even point lies at minimum AC, not why profit is only normal.

questions.stem_md: True or false? A competitive firm should stop producing in the short run as soon as price falls below average cost.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** It should stop only when price falls below minimum AVC. Between minimum AVC and minimum AC it makes a loss but a smaller one than its fixed cost by producing.

questions.stem_md: The point where price equals minimum average variable cost is called the ___ point.
questions.solution_md: It is the shut-down point: below it the firm stops production in the short run.

questions.stem_md: An imagined Rajkot brass-fittings unit has AC = Q² − 10Q + 40 + 72/Q and MC = 3Q² − 20Q + 40 (₹ hundred, Q in hundreds). Given that MC = AC at Q = 6, find the break-even price.
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: AC at Q = 6 = 36 − 60 + 40 + 12 = 28.
Step 2: MC at 6 = 108 − 120 + 40 = 28, equal to AC, so AC is at its minimum.
Step 3: Break-even price = minimum AC = ₹28 hundred.

questions.stem_md:
An imagined Erode turmeric-powder unit sells in a competitive market at ₹33 per hundred packets. Its total costs are given below. Find its maximum profit (in ₹).

| Output (hundred packets) | TC (₹) |
|---|---|
| 0 | 36 |
| 1 | 60 |
| 2 | 78 |
| 3 | 93 |
| 4 | 111 |
| 5 | 135 |
| 6 | 168 |
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: MC = 24, 18, 15, 18, 24, 33.
Step 2: MC = MR = 33 at output 6 with MC rising.
Step 3: Profit = 33 × 6 − 168 = 198 − 168 = 30. So ₹30.

questions.stem_md:
The market price for the imagined Erode turmeric-powder unit falls to ₹24 per hundred packets. With the total costs below, what is the smallest loss (in ₹) it can make by producing?

| Output (hundred packets) | TC (₹) |
|---|---|
| 0 | 36 |
| 1 | 60 |
| 2 | 78 |
| 3 | 93 |
| 4 | 111 |
| 5 | 135 |
| 6 | 168 |
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: MC = MR = 24 with MC rising at output 5.
Step 2: TR = 24 × 5 = 120; TC = 135.
Step 3: Loss = 135 − 120 = 15, less than TFC of 36, so it keeps producing. Smallest loss = ₹15.

questions.stem_md: Arrange the steps a competitive firm follows to decide its short-run output, in the correct order.

options.text_md: Produce that output if price covers AVC; otherwise shut down
Take the market price as given: AR = MR = price
Compare price with AVC at that output
Find the output where MC = MR with MC rising

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (b) → (d) → (c) → (a). The firm accepts the market price, finds the MC = MR output, then checks the price against AVC before deciding to produce or shut down.

marking_scheme.step: Complete correct sequence (all items in place)

questions.stem_md: State the two conditions of equilibrium of a firm and explain why each is needed.
questions.solution_md: Both conditions with reasons.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **MC = MR:** while MR exceeds MC, one more unit **adds to profit**; where MC exceeds MR, cutting output raises profit.
2. **MC rising:** if MC were still falling, the **next units** would add more to revenue than to cost, so profit would not yet peak.

questions.stem_md: Price in the imagined Rajkot brass market is ₹47 hundred and the unit produces 7 hundred fittings at an AC of about ₹29.29 hundred. Does it earn supernormal profit? Explain with figures.
questions.solution_md: AR above AC, with total profit computed.

answer.model_answer_md: Yes. **Price (AR) ₹47 hundred exceeds AC ₹29.29 hundred**, so each hundred fittings earns about ₹17.71 hundred above all costs including normal profit. Total supernormal profit = TR 329 − TC 205 = **₹124 hundred**.

questions.stem_md: The imagined Erode turmeric-powder unit (TFC ₹36) finds that at a price of ₹18 its best output gives a loss of ₹39. Should it produce? Give reasons.
questions.solution_md: Compare the loss with TFC; price below minimum AVC.

answer.model_answer_md: No. Producing loses **₹39**, while shutting down loses only the **fixed cost of ₹36**. Price ₹18 is **below minimum AVC (₹18.75)**, so revenue does not cover variable cost; the unit should **shut down** in the short run.

marking_scheme.step: Price below minimum AVC, shut down

questions.stem_md: For the imagined Rajkot brass unit (minimum AVC ₹15 hundred, minimum AC ₹28 hundred), state what kind of short-run result it earns at prices of ₹47, ₹28 and ₹20 hundred, with reasons.
questions.solution_md: Each price placed relative to AC and AVC.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **₹47 hundred:** price is **above AC** at the MC = MR output, so the unit earns **supernormal profit**.
2. **₹28 hundred:** price **equals minimum AC**; TR = TC, so it earns **only normal profit** (break-even).
3. **₹20 hundred:** price is **below AC but above AVC**; it makes a **loss** but keeps producing, as revenue covers variable cost and part of fixed cost.

questions.stem_md: With a described diagram, show a perfectly competitive firm making a loss in the short run while continuing to produce.
questions.solution_md: Described diagram with the loss area and the AVC condition.

answer.model_answer_md: Draw **AC, AVC and MC** (U-shaped) with a horizontal **AR = MR** line set **below minimum AC** but **above minimum AVC**. Equilibrium is at **E**, where **MC = MR** and MC is rising; output is **OQ**. At OQ, **AC lies above AR**, so the rectangle between AC and AR up to OQ shows the **loss**. An imagined Erode turmeric-powder unit has these marginal costs per hundred packets. At a market price of ₹24, find its equilibrium output, and explain why it does not stop at the 1st hundred.

| Output (hundred packets) | MC (₹) |
|---|---|
| 1 | 24 |
| 2 | 18 |
| 3 | 15 |
| 4 | 18 |
| 5 | 24 |
| 6 | 33 |
questions.solution_md: Two MC = MR points; choose the one with MC rising.

answer.model_answer_md: MC = MR = ₹24 at the **1st** and the **5th** hundred packets. At the 1st, MC is **falling** (next MCs 18, 15), so producing more **adds to profit**. At the **5th**, MC = 24 and is **rising** (next MC 33 > 24), so profit is greatest there: **equilibrium output = 5 hundred packets**.

questions.stem_md: Explain, with described diagrams, the short-run equilibrium of a firm under perfect competition when it earns (i) supernormal profit, (ii) normal profit and (iii) a loss.
questions.solution_md: Common conditions, three cases with diagram descriptions, and the reason for producing at a loss.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Common features:** the firm faces a horizontal **AR = MR** at the market price; it produces where **MC = MR** with MC **rising**; AC and AVC are U-shaped and MC cuts them at their minima.
2. **Supernormal profit:** AR = MR lies **above minimum AC**; at the equilibrium output AR exceeds AC, and the rectangle between them shows the profit.
3. **Normal profit:** AR = MR is **tangent to minimum AC**; MC = MR = AC there, so TR = TC: the **break-even point**.
4. **Loss:** AR = MR lies **below minimum AC** but **above minimum AVC**; AC exceeds AR at equilibrium and the rectangle shows the loss.
5. **Why produce at a loss:** revenue covers **all variable cost** and part of fixed cost, so the loss is smaller than closing down.

marking_scheme.step: Reason for producing at a loss

questions.stem_md:
An imagined Erode turmeric-powder unit (TFC ₹36) has the total costs below. Answer both parts. [2 + 3]

| Output (hundred packets) | TC (₹) |
|---|---|
| 0 | 36 |
| 1 | 60 |
| 2 | 78 |
| 3 | 93 |
| 4 | 111 |
| 5 | 135 |
| 6 | 168 |

(a) Find its equilibrium output and profit at a price of ₹33.
(b) At a price of ₹18, compare the loss from producing its best output with the loss from shutting down, and advise the owner.
questions.solution_md: MC from TC; MC = MR; profit; loss compared with TFC; shut-down rule.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) MC = 24, 18, 15, 18, 24, 33. MC = MR = 33 at **output 6** with MC rising. Profit = 33 × 6 − 168 = **₹30**.
(b) At ₹18, MC = MR with MC rising at **output 4**: TR = 72 and TC = 111, so the loss is **₹39**. Shutting down loses only the **fixed cost of ₹36**. Price ₹18 is **below minimum AVC (₹18.75 at output 4)**, so revenue does not cover variable cost. The owner should **shut down for now** and restart when price rises above ₹18.75.

questions.stem_md:
An imagined Rajkot brass-fittings unit in a competitive market has a minimum AVC of ₹15 hundred at 5 hundred fittings and a minimum AC of ₹28 hundred at 6 hundred. Answer both parts. [2 + 3]

(a) Explain its break-even point and shut-down point with a described diagram.
(b) The market price falls from ₹28 to ₹20 hundred. Evaluate whether the unit should stay open, using these figures.
questions.solution_md: Both points defined and placed; decision using AVC, AC and TFC.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The **break-even point** is where AR = MR **touches minimum AC** (₹28 hundred, output 6): TR = TC and only normal profit is earned. The **shut-down point** is where AR = MR **touches minimum AVC** (₹15 hundred, output 5): revenue just covers variable cost, and the loss equals fixed cost.
(b) At ₹20 hundred the price is **below minimum AC** (28), so the unit makes a **loss**. But it is **above minimum AVC** (15), so revenue covers all variable cost and part of the **fixed cost of ₹72 hundred**; the loss of about ₹46 hundred is smaller than 72. It should **stay open in the short run**, but if the price stays below ₹28 hundred it may leave the industry in the long run.

marking_scheme.step: (b) Price above AVC: covers variable cost

questions.stem_md: In the long run, a firm under perfect competition earns

options.text_md: only normal profit
supernormal profit for ever
a loss equal to its fixed cost
profit equal to its total revenue

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** only normal profit. Free entry removes supernormal profit and free exit removes losses, so in the long run firms earn only normal profit with price equal to minimum long-run average cost.

questions.stem_md: Firms producing an imagined variety of incense sticks in a competitive market are earning supernormal profit. What will most likely happen in the long run?

options.text_md: Existing firms raise the price to protect their profit
Firms leave the industry because demand falls
The price rises because more firms compete for buyers
New firms enter, market supply rises and price falls until only normal profit is left

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** New firms enter, market supply rises and price falls until only normal profit is left. Supernormal profit attracts entrants; the rise in market supply lowers price until P = minimum AC and profit is only normal.

questions.stem_md: True or false? In long-run equilibrium under perfect competition, price equals the minimum of the firm's long-run average cost.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** With only normal profit left, P = AR = MR = MC = minimum LAC in the long run.

questions.stem_md: Explain how free exit removes losses from a perfectly competitive industry in the long run.
questions.solution_md: Exit, supply falls, price rises to minimum AC.

answer.model_answer_md: If firms are making **losses**, some **leave** the industry. Market **supply falls**, so the **price rises**. Exit continues until the price covers **average cost** again and the remaining firms earn **normal profit**.

questions.stem_md: Without a diagram, explain why a firm under perfect competition earns only normal profit in the long run.
questions.solution_md: Entry, exit and the end point.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Supernormal profit** in the short run attracts **new firms**, because entry is free; market supply rises and **price falls**.
2. **Losses** make some firms **leave**, because exit is free; supply falls and **price rises**.
3. Entry and exit stop only when price equals **minimum long-run average cost**, so each firm earns **just normal profit** and has no reason to enter or leave.

marking_scheme.step: End point: P = minimum LAC, normal profit

questions.stem_md:
Firms producing imagined clay water-pots in a competitive district market earn supernormal profit this summer. Answer both parts. [2 + 3]

(a) State the short-run equilibrium conditions behind this profit.
(b) Evaluate the claim that the potters can expect the same profit every summer, explaining the long-run adjustment in words.
questions.solution_md: Conditions; entry lowers price to minimum AC; judgement.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Each potter produces where **MC = MR (= price)** with **MC rising**; the price lies **above AC** at that output, so the firm earns supernormal profit.
(b) The claim is **unlikely** to hold. Supernormal profit is a **signal**: since entry is **free**, new potters will join and some existing ones will expand. Market **supply rises**, so the **price falls** until it equals **minimum average cost**. Then each potter earns only **normal profit**. The profit lasts only while entry takes time; in the long run it **disappears**, unless demand keeps rising faster than new supply.

marking_scheme.step: (b) Price falls to minimum AC, normal profit

questions.stem_md:
Answer both parts. [2 + 2]

(i) An imagined city has three large broadband providers who match each other's plan changes within days. Identify the market form and explain one feature shown.
(ii) Compare the demand curve faced by one of these providers with the demand curve faced by a monopolist.
questions.solution_md: Form with feature; definite versus indeterminate demand.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **Oligopoly:** only **a few** large providers, and they show **interdependence**, since each changes its plans after watching rivals.
(ii) The **monopolist** faces the whole **market demand curve**, which slopes downward and is **definite**. An oligopolist's demand curve is **indeterminate**: how much it sells after a price change depends on whether rivals **follow or not**, which cannot be known in advance.

questions.stem_md:
Answer both parts about the imagined Erode turmeric-powder unit (TFC ₹36, MC per hundred packets 24, 18, 15, 18, 24, 33). [2 + 2]

(i) Find its equilibrium output at a price of ₹33 and explain the rule you used.
(ii) Explain why it would still produce at a price of ₹24 even though it makes a loss.
questions.solution_md: MC = MR rule; loss compared with TFC and AVC.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) A competitive firm produces where **MC = MR = price** with MC **rising**. MC = 33 at the **6th** hundred packets and is rising, so equilibrium output is **6 hundred packets**.
(ii) At ₹24 it produces 5 hundred packets with a loss of **₹15**, which is **less than the fixed cost of ₹36** it would lose by closing. Price ₹24 is **above minimum AVC (₹18.75)**, so producing covers variable cost and part of fixed cost.

questions.stem_md:
Answer both parts. [4 + 4]

(i) Explain four features of perfect competition and show how together they make the firm a price taker.
(ii) Distinguish between monopolistic competition and oligopoly on four bases, using imagined Indian examples.
questions.solution_md: Four features linked to price taking; four bases of distinction with examples.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **Very many buyers and sellers:** each firm's supply is a tiny share, so it cannot move the price. **Homogeneous product:** buyers do not prefer any seller, so a higher price loses all custom. **Free entry and exit:** firms come and go, so no one can hold a special position. **Perfect knowledge:** everyone knows the ruling price, so it is uniform. Together these leave each firm to **accept the market price**: AR = MR is horizontal.
(ii) **Number of sellers:** monopolistic competition has **many**, as among an imagined town's many bakeries; oligopoly has **a few**, as among an imagined state's four cement makers. **Product:** bakeries sell **differentiated** goods; oligopolists may sell **identical or differentiated** goods. **Interdependence:** a bakery acts **largely independently**; cement makers **react to each other**. **Entry:** bakeries enter **freely**; cement making has **high barriers** such as huge capital.

questions.stem_md:
Answer both parts about an imagined Rajkot brass-fittings unit in a competitive market (minimum AVC ₹15 hundred, minimum AC ₹28 hundred, TFC ₹72 hundred). [4 + 4]

(i) With described diagrams, explain its short-run equilibrium at a price of ₹47 hundred (output 7 hundred, AC about ₹29.29 hundred) and at ₹28 hundred.
(ii) Evaluate what will happen to the unit and the industry in the long run if the price of ₹47 hundred persists for a while.
questions.solution_md: Two equilibria with diagrams; long-run entry and its effects.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) At **₹47 hundred**, AR = MR is a horizontal line above minimum AC. Equilibrium is where **MC = MR** with MC rising, at **7 hundred** fittings. AR exceeds AC (about ₹29.29 hundred), so the rectangle between them shows **supernormal profit** of about **₹124 hundred**. At **₹28 hundred**, AR = MR **touches minimum AC** at 6 hundred fittings; MC = MR = AC, TR = TC, and the unit earns **only normal profit**, the break-even point.
(ii) A price of ₹47 hundred gives supernormal profit, which **attracts new firms**, since entry is free; existing firms may also expand. **Market supply rises** and the price **falls**. Entry continues until the price equals **minimum average cost**, so the unit is left with **normal profit**. The supernormal profit is therefore **temporary**; how long it lasts depends on how quickly new units can be set up. Buyers gain from the **lower price** and larger output.

questions.stem_md: Read the imagined student field notes about three markets in Nashik and answer the questions that follow. *(Written by SOYL for practice; the markets and firms are imagined.)*

**(a)** **Correct option: (a)** Perfect competition. Many sellers of an identical product who take the ruling price.

**(b)** Few sellers reacting to each other.

**(c) (i)** Form with two evidenced features.

**OR (c) (ii)** Many sellers, homogeneous product, price taker.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** (a) Perfect competition

**(b)** **Oligopoly**: "the other two announced similar offers within a week" shows **interdependence**.
